displayQuote: You will not be punished for your anger; you will be punished by your anger

meta.title: Who really said "You will not be punished for your anger"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not the Buddha. It began as Eknath Easwaran's 1993 paraphrase of Buddhist teaching on karma — 'we are not punished for our anger, we are punished by our anger' — and hardened into a fake quotation once later writers changed 'we' to 'you' and put it in quotation marks.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You will not be punished for your anger'?
meta.ogDescription: A paraphrase that became a quotation. Eknath Easwaran wrote it about the Buddha in 1993; within three years other books were printing it as the Buddha's own words.

answer.label: Not the Buddha — a 1993 paraphrase that hardened into a quote
answer.sourceLine: No Pali source exists. The sentence starts life as a paraphrase: in 1993, in To Love Is to Know Me, the teacher and translator Eknath Easwaran wrote that ‘the Buddha says that we are not punished for our anger, we are punished by our anger’ — a summary of Buddhist teaching on karma, explicitly in his own words. Within a year or two the ‘we’ had become ‘you’ and the summary had acquired quotation marks, appearing that way in Judith Sills’ Excess Baggage (1994) and then, as a flat attribution to the Buddha, in James Garbarino’s book of 1995 and a run of titles in 1996. You are watching a paraphrase turn into a quotation in about three years.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Not present — no verse or discourse
Eknath Easwaran, To Love Is to Know Me (1993) — as paraphrase
Mid-1990s; in print as the Buddha’s words by 1995
Dhammapada 223 — and it says something else

source.excerpt: Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!
trail: The canon says no. There is no Dhammapada verse and no Nikaya discourse containing this sentence. What the Dhammapada does have is a whole run of verses on anger — verse 222 on holding back rising anger like a rolling chariot, verse 223 quoted above, verse 224 on not yielding to it — and none of them frames anger as a punishment read them free ↗.

The paper trail is unusually tidy. 1993: Easwaran paraphrases, in the third person, with no quotation marks. 1994: Judith Sills’ Excess Baggage carries a version with the pronoun switched. 1995: James Garbarino’s Raising Children in a Socially Toxic Environment attributes it to the Buddha outright. 1996: it is in several more books at once, and after that the internet does the rest the year-by-year trace ↗.

The pronoun is the fingerprint. Easwaran wrote ‘we’ — the inclusive voice of a teacher describing a shared condition. The version everyone quotes says ‘you’, which turns a description into an admonishment. That single-letter edit is the moment it stopped being commentary and started being scripture.
source.excerptNote: The genuine verse on anger, in Müller’s 1881 English. Note that it is an instruction, not a warning: overcome anger with love. The quotation on this page instead makes anger its own penalty — a neat, quotable idea, and one the Dhammapada never advances.

source.rightsNote: Two different rights situations sit on this page. The Dhammapada excerpt is free — Müller’s 1881 translation is public domain worldwide. The quotation itself is not ancient and should not be treated as free: it derives from Eknath Easwaran’s 1993 prose, which remains in copyright, and the ‘you’ form was shaped by later authors whose books are also in copyright. A single aphoristic sentence quoted with attribution is a normal, ordinary use; reprinting it as if it were unowned scripture is the thing to avoid. Because we cannot cleanly assign the modern wording to one holder, we make no rights claim about it. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Gautama Buddha
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on the Buddha
author.metaLine: c. 5th century BCE · founder of Buddhism · northern India
author.bio: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught in northern India in roughly the fifth century BCE, and anger is one of the subjects his recorded teaching returns to most often — the Dhammapada devotes a chapter to it. That genuine emphasis is exactly what makes the misattribution stick: a reader who knows the Buddha talked about anger has no reason to doubt a sentence that talks about anger well. The irony is that the good modern sentence displaces the actual verses, which are stranger and more demanding than ‘anger hurts you’.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is one of the cleanest case studies we have of how a fake quotation is actually made. Nobody forged anything. A teacher summarised a doctrine, a later writer tidied the pronoun, an editor added quotation marks, and thirty years on it outranks the real verses in search results.

items.why: Not in the Dhammapada, not in the Nikayas. The Dhammapada’s own anger verses (221–224) prescribe overcoming anger with love and non-yielding — they do not describe it as self-inflicted punishment.

In To Love Is to Know Me he writes that the Buddha says we are not punished for our anger but by it. That is a teacher glossing karma in his own words — a perfectly honest thing to do, and not a translation of anything the trace ↗.

Judith Sills’ Excess Baggage (1994) carries the switched-pronoun form. Inclusive commentary becomes direct address, and direct address sounds like someone speaking — which invites quotation marks, which invites a speaker.
By 1995 it is in print credited to the Buddha; in 1996 it appears in several books at once. After that no individual author is responsible for it and the correction never catches up.

items.scope: What is actually true in it
items.why: Karma as consequence rather than external penalty is genuine Buddhist teaching, and Easwaran was summarising it fairly. The error is not the idea — it is the quotation marks.

misattribution.truthLine: Not the Buddha. Eknath Easwaran’s 1993 paraphrase, republished with a changed pronoun and quotation marks until it became a quotation the trace ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It reframes anger as a bad deal rather than a sin, which is far more persuasive to a modern reader. Nobody is threatening you; the arithmetic is simply against you, and you can check it yourself the next time you spend an afternoon furious at someone who has no idea.

The for/by construction is also just a very good piece of writing — two identical clauses hinged on a single preposition. That is a rhetorician’s move, not a translator’s, and it is one of the clues that no Pali original is hiding behind it.
context.detailsSummary: How a paraphrase becomes a quotation
detailsBody: 1993: Easwaran writes 'the Buddha says that we are not punished for our anger, we are punished by our anger' — his summary, in his voice.
1994: the line appears in Judith Sills' Excess Baggage with 'we' changed to 'you'.
1995: James Garbarino's book attributes it to the Buddha directly.
1996: several more titles carry it, and the original paraphrase is no longer visible behind them.
The whole mechanism takes three years and requires nobody to lie.
context.pull: Nobody forged it. Somebody changed 'we' to 'you' and added quotation marks.
